# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was twenty-three when the war came to Kyiv. He had been working as a junior sales representative for a telecommunications company, a job that felt like the natural next step after university—comfortable, unremarkable, the kind of work that let him think about his girlfriend Elena and weekend plans rather than the future in any grander sense. In February 2022, when the first explosions shook the city before dawn, he was still in that ordinary headspace, unable to fully process that the distant sounds of conflict he'd heard on the news were now happening outside his apartment building.

The first weeks were chaotic in ways that felt almost unreal. Marcus sheltered in a basement with neighbors, listening to the percussion of shelling, feeling the building tremble. What stayed with him most vividly was the particular quality of not knowing—the waiting between sounds, the impossibility of predicting what would happen next, the way a sudden loud noise would send his heart into his throat. After two months of escalating danger and dwindling supplies, Marcus made the decision to leave. He took a bus westward with a backpack and documents, watching the landscape shift from urban destruction to countryside, then crossing into Poland. From there, through a network of relatives and aid organizations, he eventually made his way to the United States on a humanitarian visa.

He arrived in Chicago in May, moving in with a distant cousin and trying to rebuild some version of normalcy. By August, he had found work again—sales for an office equipment distributor, a job that required him to be in the field, visiting clients, making calls, maintaining the kind of professional composure that felt increasingly impossible to sustain. What frightened Marcus most was the unpredictability that had become woven into his nervous system. Loud noises—a car backfiring, a door slamming, construction sounds from the street—would flood him with a surge of fear so intense that his hands would shake and his breath would come shallow. He had come to believe that danger was fundamentally unpredictable, that safety was an illusion, and that he needed to be vigilant at all times to protect himself.

The night was the worst. As darkness fell, Marcus felt a shift in his body that he couldn't quite control. His apartment, which felt reasonably secure during daylight hours, became a place of heightened alertness after sunset. He found himself checking locks multiple times, keeping lights on, unable to settle into sleep until exhaustion overwhelmed him around three or four in the morning. He was certain that nighttime was when bad things happened—when you couldn't see threats coming, when help felt farther away. His girlfriend Elena, who had moved in with him in September, began to notice the pattern. She would wake to find him sitting in the dark living room, or she would feel him tense beside her at the slightest sound. When she tried to reassure him, to remind him that they were safe in Chicago, that the war was thousands of miles away, something in him couldn't accept it. The reassurance felt naive, even dangerous—a failure to stay alert.

At work, the difficulty concentrating had begun to affect his performance. During client meetings, his mind would drift or fracture, unable to hold the thread of a conversation about printer specifications or service contracts. His manager had pulled him aside twice in recent weeks, noting that his sales numbers had dropped significantly and that he seemed "distant" or "checked out." Marcus couldn't explain it in a way that made sense to someone who hadn't lived through what he had. How could he tell his manager that the fluorescent lights and the hum of the office felt like they were vibrating at a frequency that made his chest tight? That concentrating on work felt like a luxury he couldn't afford because part of his mind was always scanning for the next threat?

At twenty-five, Marcus came to therapy because Elena had insisted, and because he was beginning to suspect that he couldn't fix this alone. What he wanted most was to feel safe again, to be able to sleep through the night without his body jolting awake at phantom sounds. What he feared most was that the person he had been before February 2022 was gone for good, replaced by someone hypervigilant and fractured, someone who couldn't be present in his own life.
